query: What concrete contamination controls, monitoring protocols, and geographic/temporal buffers minimize spillovers between treatment and control clusters in local markets?

response.query: What concrete contamination controls, monitoring protocols, and geographic/temporal buffers minimize spillovers between treatment and control clusters in local markets?
response.answer: Concrete contamination controls include physical separation, strict monitoring, and buffer zones. Regular audits and geographic/temporal buffers minimize spillovers between treatment and control clusters.

results.title: Understanding Labour Shortages: The Structural Forces at ...
results.content: Against this background, this chapter builds on the new GFP Employer Survey findings, complemented by administrative data, to explore the intensity and nature of labour and skill shortages across OECD countries, and outlines policies that can help to alleviate shortages. Labour markets are cooling after significant tightness during the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, yet labour shortages persist and are severe in high-skilled jobs and in occupations characterised by low pay and strenuous working conditions. (2023), “The effects of the EU Fit for 55 package on labour markets and the demand for skills*”, OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers*, No. 297, OECD Publishing, Paris. Tanaka (2024a), “Labour shortages and labour market inequalities: evidence and policy implications”, *OECD Economics Department Working Papers*, OECD Publishing, Paris, forthcoming. Tanaka (2024b), "Labour markets transitions in the greening economy: structural drivers and the role of policies", *OECD Economics Department Working Papers*, No. 1803, OECD Publishing, Paris.

results.title: Under pressure: Labour market and wage developments in ...
results.content: The recent decline in energy prices and the improving prospects for China have contributed to an uptake in economic indicators in the first half of 2023, with global GDP growth picking up to an annualised rate of just over 3% in the first quarter, despite mixed outcomes across countries and particularly weak growth in the Euro Area [(OECD, 2023[2])](/en/publications/oecd-employment-outlook-2023_08785bba-en/full-report/under-pressure-labour-market-and-wage-developments-in-oecd-countries_dd4dbb5b.html#Kappa_ce188438_daef2e6397). However, the increase in profit margins does not necessarily imply an *increase* in the market-power of firms – as captured by the percentage mark-up of prices over the marginal cost [(Colonna, Torrini and Viviano, 2023[62])](/en/publications/oecd-employment-outlook-2023_08785bba-en/full-report/under-pressure-labour-market-and-wage-developments-in-oecd-countries_dd4dbb5b.html#Mendeley_LdIn4rFT4jS_YrHC9KeQ0Q_daef2e6397). Moreover, the increasing body of evidence across OECD countries on monopsony power, i.e. firms’ power to set wages unilaterally leading to inefficiently low levels of employment and wages, has reinforced the arguments for raising the minimum wage where it is too low, or introducing one where it does not exist, in particular when workers are not already covered by effective collective bargaining [(OECD, 2022[54])](/en/publications/oecd-employment-outlook-2023_08785bba-en/full-report/under-pressure-labour-market-and-wage-developments-in-oecd-countries_dd4dbb5b.html#Kappa_1bb305a6_daef2e6397).
